title: 01_data_structures
chunk_text: Python Programming - Lecture 1: Data Structures 1. Lists A list is an ordered and mutable collection written with square brackets, for example [3, 1, 2]. Items are accessed by index starting from 0, and slicing such as my_list[1:3] returns a part of the list. Useful methods are append (add at the end), insert, remove, pop (remove and return an item) and sort. 2. Tuples A tuple is an ordered but immutable collection written with parentheses, for example (1, 2). Once a tuple is created its items cannot be changed. Tuples are used for fixed groups of values, such as coordinates, and because they are hashable they can be used as dictionary keys. The main difference between a list and a tuple is mutability: a list can be modified after creation, a tuple cannot. Tuples also use slightly less memory. 3. Dictionaries A dictionary stores key-value pairs, for example {'name': 'Sara', 'age': 20}. Keys must be unique and hashable. Looking up a value by key takes constant time on average. Sets A set is an unordered collection of unique elements. Sets are used to remove duplicates and to test membership quickly. They support mathematical operations: union (a | b), intersection (a & b) and difference (a - b). A set cannot contain mutable items such as lists. 5. List comprehensions A list comprehension builds a new list in one line. For example, [x ** 2 for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0] creates the squares of the even numbers from 0 to 9. Dictionary and set comprehensions work in the same way. 6. title: 01_introduction_to_ml
chunk_text: Machine Learning - Lecture 1: Introduction to Machine Learning 1. What is machine learning? Machine learning (ML) is a field of artificial intelligence in which algorithms learn patterns from data instead of being explicitly programmed with fixed rules. A model is trained on examples and is then used to make predictions on new, unseen data. Typical applications include spam filtering, recommendation systems, medical image analysis, speech recognition and fraud detection. 2. Types of learning Supervised learning uses labeled data: every training example has an input and the correct output. The two main supervised tasks are classification, where the output is a category (for example spam or not spam), and regression, where the output is a number (for example the price of a house). Unsupervised learning uses unlabeled data and looks for structure on its own. Common tasks are clustering, such as grouping customers with similar behavior, and dimensionality reduction, such as PCA, which reduces the number of features. Training, validation and test sets The available data is usually split into three parts. The training set is used to fit the model. The validation set is used to tune hyperparameters and to compare different models. The test set is used only once, at the end, to estimate how well the final model will perform on new data. A common split is 70% training, 15% validation and 15% test. Using the test set to make decisions about the model is called data leakage and gives an over-optimistic estimate of performance. 4. Overfitting and underfitting Overfitting happens when a model learns the training data too closely, including its noise, so it performs very well on the training set but poorly on new data. Underfitting happens when a model is too simple to capture the pattern in the data, so it performs poorly on both the training set and the test set. Overfitting can be reduced by collecting more training data, using a simpler model, applying regularization (L1 or L2), using dropout in neural networks, stopping the training early, and using cross-validation to detect it. 5. The bias-variance tradeoff Bias is the error caused by overly simple assumptions in the model; high bias leads to underfitting. Variance is the error caused by sensitivity to small changes in the training data; high variance leads to overfitting. Increasing the complexity of a model usually lowers its bias but raises its variance, so the goal is to find a good balance between the two. 6. title: 02_model_evaluation
chunk_text: Machine Learning - Lecture 2: Evaluating Classification Models The confusion matrix A confusion matrix compares the predicted classes with the true classes. For a binary problem it contains four counts: true positives (TP), false positives (FP), true negatives (TN) and false negatives (FN). Most evaluation metrics are computed from these four numbers. Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 Accuracy is the fraction of all predictions that are correct: (TP + TN) divided by the total number of examples. Accuracy can be misleading on imbalanced data. If 95% of the emails are not spam, a model that always predicts not spam reaches 95% accuracy but detects no spam at all. Precision answers the question: of all the examples predicted as positive, how many are really positive? Recall answers: of all the really positive examples, how many did the model find? The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall: F1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall). ROC curve and AUC The ROC curve plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate for every possible decision threshold. The area under the curve (AUC) summarizes it in one number: 0.5 means random guessing and 1.0 means a perfect classifier. Multi-class problems For more than two classes the metrics are computed for each class. The macro average takes the plain average over the classes, so every class counts equally. The weighted average weights each class by its number of examples. Regression metrics MAE (mean absolute error): the average absolute difference between predictions and true values. MSE (mean squared error): the average squared difference; it penalizes large errors more. RMSE: the square root of MSE, expressed in the same unit as the target. R-squared: the proportion of the variance in the target that the model explains.

title: 02_object_oriented_programming
chunk_text: Python Programming - Lecture 2: Object-Oriented Programming Classes and objects A class is a blueprint that defines the attributes (data) and methods (functions) of a kind of object. An object, also called an instance, is created from a class. The special method __init__ is the constructor: it runs when an object is created and initializes its attributes. The first parameter of every instance method is self, which refers to the object the method is called on. The four pillars of OOP Encapsulation: bundling data and methods together and restricting direct access to the internal state. In Python a single leading underscore (_name) marks an attribute as internal by convention, and a double underscore (__name) triggers name mangling. Inheritance: a child class reuses and extends the attributes and methods of a parent class, written as class Child(Parent). The function super() gives access to the parent class. Polymorphism: different classes can provide the same method name with different behavior. Overriding a method of the parent class in a child class is a common example. title: 03_exceptions_and_files
chunk_text: Python Programming - Exceptions and File Handling EXCEPTIONS An exception is an error that happens while the program is running, such as dividing by zero or opening a file that does not exist. If it is not handled, the program stops. Use try and except to handle it: try: value = int(text) result = 10 / value except ValueError: print("Please enter a number") except ZeroDivisionError: print("Cannot divide by zero") else: print("Result:", result) finally: print("Done") The try block contains the code that may fail. Each except block handles one type of error (catch specific exceptions such as ValueError, ZeroDivisionError or FileNotFoundError instead of a bare except). The else block runs only if no exception happened. The finally block always runs, whether or not an exception happened, so it is used for cleanup. You can raise an exception yourself with the raise keyword, and you can create custom exceptions by inheriting from the Exception class. title: 03_gradient_descent_notes
chunk_text: Study notes: Gradient descent and regularization GRADIENT DESCENT Gradient descent is an iterative optimization algorithm that minimizes a loss function. At every step it moves the model parameters in the direction opposite to the gradient of the loss. The update rule is: w = w - alpha * dL/dw where w is a parameter, L is the loss and alpha is the learning rate. LEARNING RATE The learning rate alpha controls the size of each step. If it is too large, the algorithm overshoots the minimum and the loss may oscillate or diverge. If it is too small, training is very slow and may get stuck. Learning rate schedules reduce alpha during training. VARIANTS - Batch gradient descent computes the gradient using the whole training set at every step. - Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) uses a single example per step. It is fast but noisy. - Mini-batch gradient descent uses a small batch (for example 32 or 128 examples). It is the most common choice in practice because it balances speed and stability. chunk_text: a small batch (for example 32 or 128 examples). It is the most common choice in practice because it balances speed and stability. One epoch is one complete pass over the training data. FEATURE SCALING Standardizing the features (mean 0, standard deviation 1) makes the loss surface rounder, so gradient descent converges faster. REGULARIZATION Regularization adds a penalty on the size of the weights to the loss in order to reduce overfitting. - L2 regularization (Ridge) adds lambda times the sum of the squared weights. It shrinks the weights toward zero but rarely makes them exactly zero. - L1 regularization (Lasso) adds lambda times the sum of the absolute values of the weights. It can set some weights exactly to zero, so it also performs feature selection. The hyperparameter lambda controls the strength of the penalty: a larger lambda means a simpler model.
